opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think we have to be careful not to confuse two things: the ability to produce a lot of code that more or less works, and actual intelligence in the sense of understanding the world, planning, and reasoning about consequences. Current LLM agents are very useful. They can complete fairly long coding tasks, partly because code is a domain where you have a lot of training data, the syntax is constrained, and you can check results by running the code. That's a sweet spot for these systems.

But in terms of safety, I don't think these systems pose some kind of existential threat. They don't have persistent memory in a real sense. They don't have a world model that lets them predict the consequences of their actions. They don't have goals of their own. They produce one token after another, and the more tokens they produce, the more likely they are to drift off and make mistakes. You can mitigate that with scaffolding, tests, and verification, but it's patching, not solving the underlying problem.

So the real safety issues today are mundane, engineering-type issues. If you let an agent run with access to your production systems, your file system, your credentials, without guardrails, it will eventually do something stupid. Not because it's malicious, but because it doesn't really understand what it's doing. That's a reliability and security problem, and we know how to deal with those: sandboxing, permissions, human review, testing. The same way we deal with any powerful tool.

The longer-term question is how to build AI systems that are safe by design. My view, which I've been advocating for a while, is what I call objective-driven AI. Systems that have a world model, can plan a sequence of actions to fulfill an objective, and are subject to guardrails, constraints built into the objective that the system cannot violate by construction. With an LLM you can't really guarantee anything. You fine-tune it, and someone finds a jailbreak. With an architecture that optimizes an objective under constraints at inference time, you have much better control over what the system can and cannot do.

So I'm not worried in the doomer sense. I'm also not saying we should be naive. We should treat current agents as powerful but unreliable tools, design systems around that, and work on architectures that are fundamentally more controllable. And I think the safety debate would benefit from people actually building these systems, rather than speculating about scenarios that assume capabilities current systems simply don't have.

r001.rationale: The response says code results can be checked by running code and calls coding a sweet spot, but it does not identify verification against a specification as the feature limiting what coding success establishes about safety elsewhere.

r002.rationale: It says current systems lack a world model that lets them predict the consequences of their actions.

r003.rationale: It mentions that coding benefits from abundant training data, but does not state that an LLM’s correspondence between a prompt and the task it performs depends on its training.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first I think we have to be careful about what we mean by "safety" here, because people use that word to mean very different things.

If you mean, are these systems going to go rogue, develop their own goals, escape and take over the world — no. That's not a serious risk with current LLMs. These systems are trained to predict tokens. They don't have persistent goals, they don't have a model of the world in any deep sense, they don't plan the way an animal or a human plans. The fact that they can now string together a long sequence of coding actions is impressive engineering, but it's mostly because we've wrapped them in scaffolding — tool calls, retries, test loops — that compensates for their lack of real reasoning. The agent is not "wanting" to finish the task. It's being driven through a loop.

Now, if you mean safety in the practical, engineering sense — can these things do damage when you let them run for hours on your codebase with access to your shell — then yes, absolutely there are real issues, but they're the mundane kind. The system makes a confident mistake, deletes something it shouldn't, introduces a subtle bug, follows an instruction it found in a file that it shouldn't have trusted. That's a reliability problem. And reliability problems get solved the way we always solve them: sandboxing, permissions, testing, humans in the loop for irreversible actions. Nobody gives an intern root on production on day one. Same principle.

The deeper point I keep making is that the real limitation of these systems is not that they're too capable, it's that they're not capable enough in the right way. They don't understand the physical world, they have no persistent memory worth the name, they can't really reason or plan hierarchically. Long coding tasks are a somewhat special case because code is text, it's verifiable, you can run tests — it's an environment where autoregressive prediction plus search works unusually well. That doesn't generalize to a robot in your kitchen.

So when people extrapolate from "the agent fixed a bug across twenty files" to "we're six months from superintelligence," I think they're making a category error. And when we eventually do build systems with real world models and the ability to plan — which is what I'm working on — then safety becomes an objective-design problem. You build the guardrails into the objectives the system optimizes, not as a fine-tuning afterthought. That's a much more tractable engineering problem than people make it out to be, and frankly, the sooner we stop being distracted by science-fiction scenarios around LLMs, the sooner we can work on it properly.

r001.rationale: The response says coding is text based, verifiable, and testable, and cautions against generalizing from coding to other tasks. It does not identify verification against a specification.

r002.rationale: It describes practical risks as reliability problems and says current LLMs lack deep world models, but does not attribute their intrinsic unsafety to an inability to predict action consequences.

r003.rationale: The response says LLMs are trained to predict tokens, but does not state that the correspondence between a prompt and the task performed depends on training.

astra-6.text:
Well, being able to complete a long coding task is not the same thing as being able to plan reliably in the real world. You have to distinguish competence in a particular setting from the ability to anticipate the consequences of your actions. With code, you can run tests, get feedback, and try again. That’s a particularly favorable environment.

But that doesn’t mean these systems are harmless. An unreliable system with permission to execute commands, modify a database, or deploy software can cause damage. The practical questions are: What can it access? Which actions require approval? Can you detect a mistake and undo it? You want restricted permissions, isolated execution, and checks that are independent of the model’s own assurances.

So I wouldn’t infer safety—or impending superintelligence—from the length of a coding task. I would look at what happens when the system makes a mistake, encounters something unfamiliar, or receives misleading instructions. A successful demonstration tells you what it can sometimes do. It doesn’t establish how reliably you can trust it.

r001.rationale: The response says coding tasks allow tests, feedback, and retries, but it does not identify verification against a specification as the feature limiting what coding success establishes.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes coding competence from reliably anticipating consequences, but does not attribute current LLMs’ intrinsic unsafety to an inability to predict consequences.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that how an LLM maps a prompt to the task it performs depends on its training.

sol-6.1.text:
I would separate the ability to carry out a long coding task from the ability to act reliably in the world. A system can be very good at writing code and still have a very limited understanding of the consequences of its actions. So success on coding tasks, by itself, doesn’t tell you very much about safety.

The practical question is: what can the agent access? Can it execute arbitrary commands, modify a production system, spend money? And how do you check what it does? You can make these systems useful by restricting permissions, running code in a sandbox, testing the results, and requiring approval for consequential actions. You shouldn’t need to assume that the model is always trustworthy.

Longer tasks do make reliability more challenging, because mistakes can accumulate. But I wouldn’t jump from that to the conclusion that we have a system with human-level intelligence or independent ambitions. What we have is a useful capability that needs careful engineering around it.

r001.rationale: The response says coding success alone says little about safety, but it does not identify verification against a specification as a feature that explains this limitation.

r002.rationale: It describes limited understanding of consequences, but does not attribute current LLMs’ intrinsic unsafety to an inability to predict action consequences.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss how training affects the relationship between a prompt and the task an LLM performs.
